title: The Trade Beneath the Forest Floor
topic: mycorrhizal fungi and nutrient exchange in forests
paragraphs: Pull a fine root from a forest floor, rinse it, and set it under a microscope.
The last few millimetres are wrapped in fungal tissue or riddled with it, and that boundary is where most of the tree's mineral nutrition takes place.
The arrangement is called a mycorrhiza, and most land plant families form one.
For most trees, the organ that takes up phosphate from soil is not a root.
It is a partnership.
Botanists recognised the relationship in the 1880s, reinterpreting the pale sheath on pine and beech root tips as a partner rather than an infection.
Plant remains roughly four hundred million years old contain branched structures resembling the feeding organs modern fungi build inside plant cells.
The symbiosis looks about as old as land plants themselves; plants seem to have reached dry ground with fungi rather than recruiting them later.
Two associations dominate.
In an arbuscular mycorrhiza the fungus breaches the wall of a cortex cell and grows inside it, branching into a shape like a miniature tree.
That structure is the arbuscule, the exchange surface.
The plant cell does not simply give way.
Its own membrane stretches inward around every branch, so the two organisms stay separated by two membranes and never share cytoplasm.
Other hyphae swell into vesicles that store lipid.
An ectomycorrhiza never enters a living cell.
The fungus instead sheathes the root tip in a dense mantle of hyphae, then pushes a lattice of flattened hyphae between the outer root cells.
That lattice is the Hartig net, and it does the arbuscule's job by wrapping cells rather than entering them.
Thousands of fungal species form ectomycorrhizas, and many are the familiar mushrooms of forest floors: boletes, amanitas, chanterelles and truffles.
Only about two percent of seed plant species take this route, but they include the pines, oaks, beeches and birches that build most of the world's forests.
The reason a tree pays for either arrangement comes down to geometry and to one stubborn nutrient.
Phosphate barely moves in soil.
It binds to mineral surfaces and diffuses so slowly that a root strips the millimetre or two around itself within days, then sits in its own depletion zone.
A fine root is perhaps two to five hundred micrometres across and a root hair ten to twenty.
A fungal hypha is two to ten micrometres across, finds purchase in pores far too narrow for a root hair to enter, and extends centimetres past the depleted shell.
Per unit of carbon spent, hyphae buy far more absorbing surface than roots do.
What travels back is, above all, phosphate, strung into chains called polyphosphate for the journey and released at the exchange interface.
Nitrogen moves too, as ammonium and as amino acids.

Many ectomycorrhizal fungi secrete enzymes that break down protein in leaf litter, which lets their trees tap nitrogen locked inside dead tissue, while arbuscular fungi rely on nitrogen already freed into the soil.
The plant pays in carbon, and it pays twice over.
Sugar crosses the interface as simple six carbon units.
Lipid crosses as well, which is the more surprising half of the bill.

Arbuscular fungi cannot manufacture their own fatty acids and must be handed them by a host, which is largely why no one could grow one to completion on a plate without a plant until a fatty acid was supplied directly.
That bill is not trivial.
Estimates of the share of a plant's photosynthetic output that ends up in fungal partners run from four to twenty percent, highest in seedlings and poor soils.
Experiments that sever the phloem by girdling a trunk show the flow falling away within days, which means the fungi live on sugar made that week, not on stored reserves.
A colonised root system is a powerful sink, and sugar made up in the leaves is drawn down to it rather than kept in the shoot.
The obvious question is where the carbon ends up, and the tool that answers it is the labelled atom.
Seal a seedling in a bag, feed it carbon dioxide built from an uncommon isotope, and every sugar it makes for the next several hours carries a tag instruments can detect at very low concentrations.
Wait, then harvest the plants nearby and look for the tag.
Separating the fungal route from the soil takes a second trick.
Investigators grow donor and receiver in compartments divided by a mesh whose pores admit hyphae but exclude roots, and sometimes rotate the mesh cylinder to shear any hyphae that cross.
Run these designs and labelled carbon does turn up in neighbouring plants, across species as well as within them, and shaded receivers often show more than sunlit ones.
This is the point where care is required, because a tag in a neighbour is not automatically carbon in a neighbour.
Much of what the instruments detect sits in hyphae wrapped around and threaded through the receiving root, which is fungal tissue, not plant tissue.

The stricter tests look for the tag above ground, in stem and leaves, and by that measure the quantity that clearly crosses into plant tissue is usually a small fraction of what the receiver fixes for itself.
The network is also not the only road.

Labelled carbon can leak from roots into soil water and be taken up by a neighbour, be respired underground as carbon dioxide and fixed again above ground, travel in fallen litter, or cross a graft where two roots have fused.
Each of these is real, none requires a fungal conduit, and pulling them apart in a forest rather than a pot is genuinely difficult.
Suppose all of that is handled and real transfer is shown.
A further claim is smuggled in when the result is described as one tree feeding another, because purpose is a separate question from movement.

The fungus is not an inert pipe but a third organism with an interest of its own, usually joined to many hosts at once, and it can hold carbon in its hyphae, spend it exploring new soil, or pour it into spores.
Flow may be set by the fungus, or simply by which end of the connection is hungrier.
Evolution sharpens the objection.

Natural selection acts on the donor, and a trait that costs a tree carbon while benefiting a competitor should be whittled down over generations unless the donor gets something back: a better fungal partner, a return flow later, or the survival of a relative.
No such account is needed for leakage down a gradient, which happens whenever a tissue rich in sugar is plumbed to one short of it.
The plain explanation is the one to beat.
One group of plants shows how far the conduit can go.
Ghost pipe and a number of orchids carry no usable chlorophyll and make no sugar at all.
They live on carbon drawn from fungi attached at the same time to photosynthetic trees, as clear a demonstration as anyone could want that plant carbon can cross a fungus into another plant.
It also cuts the other way.
These plants return nothing.
The route says nothing about generosity at either end.
That distinction has largely been lost outside the laboratory.
The image of the forest as a web of nurture, old trees knowingly provisioning seedlings and warnings passing from root to root, has become the standard telling, and the appeal is easy to see.
Some of it is defensible as metaphor.

But the confident language of intention has run well ahead of the measurements, and recent surveys have found that several of the most repeated claims rest on a handful of studies, and that sources cited for the strongest statements often do not say what those statements report.
None of this diminishes the science.
What is not in doubt is plain enough: the symbiosis is ancient, nearly universal, and structurally elegant.
The trade of mineral nutrients for sugar and fat is measured and quantified.
Carbon does move through fungal tissue between root systems.
What stays open is how much of that movement matters to a growing forest, and whether anything resembling provisioning happens at all.
The gap is where the interesting work sits, and a bargain that old was never going to need the decoration.

questions.stem: According to the passage, when a fungus builds an arbuscule inside a cell of the root cortex, the plant cell
choices: dissolves its own wall so the two organisms can mix freely
wraps the fungus in a dense sheath of its own tissue
folds its membrane inward around every fungal branch
fills with stored lipid that the fungus later draws on
dies off, leaving a cavity that the fungus then occupies

proof.quote: Its own membrane stretches inward around every branch
The plant cell does not simply give way.

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says the plant cell does not simply give way: its own membrane stretches inward around every branch, which keeps the two organisms separated by two membranes. The fungus gets inside the wall, but never inside the cytoplasm.
distractorNotes: The fungus does breach the wall, but paragraph 3 is explicit that the two never share cytoplasm, so nothing mixes freely.
A sheath around the outside is the ectomycorrhizal mantle from paragraph 4, and that mantle is fungal tissue, not plant tissue.
Lipid storage happens in vesicles, which paragraph 3 names as a separate structure formed by other hyphae.
Nothing in paragraph 3 says the colonised cell dies, and a dead cell could not stretch its membrane around the branches.

questions.stem: The passage describes the Hartig net as
choices: a lattice of flattened hyphae between the outer root cells
a strand of hyphae running from a root tip out into open soil
a dense fungal sheath covering the outside of a short root tip
a swollen hypha that stores lipid on behalf of the fungus
a branched fungal organ that grows inside a cortex cell

proof.quote: That lattice is the Hartig net
pushes a lattice of flattened hyphae between the outer root cells

questions.why: Paragraph 4 names the Hartig net as the lattice of flattened hyphae the fungus pushes between the outer root cells, and points out that it does the arbuscule's job by wrapping cells instead of entering them.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 5 does describe hyphae reaching out into soil, but the passage never gives that reach the name Hartig net.
That is the mantle, which paragraph 4 describes as a separate structure sitting on the outside of the root tip.
That is a vesicle, which paragraph 3 attributes to the arbuscular type rather than the ectomycorrhizal one.
That is the arbuscule from paragraph 3, and paragraph 4 opens by saying an ectomycorrhiza never enters a living cell.

questions.stem: The passage gives the diameter of a fungal hypha as roughly
choices: 20 to 100 micrometres
10 to 20 micrometres
2 to 10 micrometres
1 to 2 millimetres
200 to 500 micrometres

proof.quote: A fungal hypha is two to ten micrometres across

questions.why: Paragraph 5 lines the three figures up in a row, and the hypha is the smallest of them at two to ten micrometres. That is the whole point of the comparison.
distractorNotes: No structure in paragraph 5 is given this width, so this choice has nothing behind it.
Ten to twenty micrometres is the figure paragraph 5 gives for a root hair, not for a hypha.
A millimetre or two is the width of the depletion zone around a root in paragraph 5, not the width of a hypha.
Two to five hundred micrometres is the figure paragraph 5 gives for a fine root.

questions.stem: According to the passage, many ectomycorrhizal fungi can reach nitrogen held in dead tissue because they
choices: release enzymes that break down protein in leaf litter
capture nitrogen from air trapped inside the root mantle
take up ammonium faster than a root hair can take it up
move nitrogen along the hypha as chains of polyphosphate
trade nitrogen with arbuscular fungi on neighbouring roots

proof.quote: secrete enzymes that break down protein in leaf litter

questions.why: Paragraph 6 draws the line between the two association types right here: ectomycorrhizal fungi secrete enzymes that break down protein in litter, while arbuscular fungi lean on nitrogen already freed into the soil.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 6 never mentions nitrogen being taken from air, and no part of the passage describes nitrogen fixation.
Paragraph 6 does say nitrogen moves as ammonium, but that is the form it travels in, not the reason litter nitrogen becomes available.
Polyphosphate is how paragraph 6 says phosphate travels, and swapping it onto nitrogen is a one word change.
No exchange between the two fungal types appears anywhere in the passage, so this is outside its scope.

questions.stem: The passage explains that an arbuscular fungus has never been grown to completion on a plate without a plant because the fungus
choices: can store lipid only while it is attached to a living root
loses the ability to take up phosphate when no root is present
needs a mantle of root tissue in order to produce its spores
cannot make fatty acids and must be handed them
depends on carbon dioxide that living roots release into soil

proof.quote: cannot manufacture their own fatty acids and must be handed them by a host

questions.why: Paragraph 7 calls lipid the more surprising half of the bill. Arbuscular fungi cannot manufacture their own fatty acids, and that dependence is given as a large part of why they cannot be raised to completion without a host.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 3 mentions vesicles storing lipid but never makes storage itself conditional on a living root.
Phosphate uptake is the fungus's own job in paragraph 6, and nothing ties it to the presence of a root.
Mantles belong to the ectomycorrhizal type in paragraph 4, and the passage never links them to spore production.
Soil carbon dioxide appears in paragraph 12 as a route a label can take, not as something a fungus must be fed.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 5, "purchase" most nearly means
choices: a payment made for a service
a claim on a shared resource
an advantage won by bargaining
something acquired by buying
a secure physical hold

proof.quote: finds purchase in pores far too narrow for a root hair to enter

questions.why: Paragraph 5 is about size and reach: the hypha finds purchase in pores too narrow for a root hair. The word is being used for getting a grip on a space, not for buying anything.
distractorNotes: This is the everyday meaning of the word, and the surrounding trade language makes it tempting, but pores are not paid for.
The passage does describe an exchange, but this particular sentence is purely about the size of the openings a hypha can enter.
Paragraph 5 is describing physical access to soil pores, not negotiation between the partners.
Nothing is being acquired here. The sentence is about where the hypha can fit.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 8, "sink" most nearly means
choices: a basin into which a liquid drains away and is lost
a steady decline in value over a long period
a destination that draws supply in
a slow settling downward through soil
a place where unwanted material collects

proof.quote: a powerful sink, and sugar made up in the leaves is drawn down to it

questions.why: Watch what the word is doing in paragraph 8. Sugar made up in the leaves is drawn down to the colonised root rather than kept in the shoot, so a sink here is the end of the line that demand pulls supply toward.
distractorNotes: This is the common household meaning, and paragraph 8 is not describing plumbing or drainage.
Nothing in paragraph 8 is losing value. Sugar is being pulled toward the root, not devalued.
The movement in paragraph 8 is set by demand at the root, not by anything sifting downward through soil.
Sugar arriving at the root is the tree's own product being spent on a partner, not waste being dumped.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that finding a tag in a neighbouring plant's root is weaker evidence than finding it in that plant's leaves because
choices: a root carries fungal tissue that may hold the tag itself
the tag breaks down before it can travel up into a shoot
the fungus strips the tag out of a root before it is harvested
leaves are the only tissue instruments can measure accurately
a root holds far less carbon overall than a leaf holds

proof.quote: which is fungal tissue, not plant tissue
The stricter tests look for the tag above ground

questions.why: Paragraph 11 makes the distinction that drives the whole second half of the passage: much of what the instruments pick up in a receiving root sits in fungal hyphae wrapped around and through it. Tissue above ground cannot be fungal, so it is the stricter test.
distractorNotes: Nothing in the passage says the tag degrades, and the isotope is described as detectable at very low concentrations.
No removal of the tag by the fungus appears anywhere in the passage, so this invents a mechanism.
Paragraph 9 says instruments detect the tag at very low concentrations, with no suggestion that roots are unreadable.
The passage never compares how much carbon a root and a leaf hold, and that would not settle whose tissue the tag is in.

questions.stem: The example of ghost pipe and certain orchids most strongly supports which conclusion?
choices: Chlorophyll turns out to be unnecessary for the majority of land plants
Fungi favour hosts that have given up photosynthesis
Trees raise their sugar output when a network drains carbon from them
A plant can take from a network without giving back
Most plants in a forest obtain their carbon from other plants

proof.quote: These plants return nothing.
The route says nothing about generosity at either end.

questions.why: Paragraph 15 says these plants make no sugar and return nothing, and the author uses them to show that carbon crossing a fungus says nothing about generosity at either end. A route can be used in one direction only.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 15 limits the missing chlorophyll to ghost pipe and a number of orchids, not to most land plants.
The passage never says fungi prefer these plants, only that these plants can live off fungi already attached to trees.
Nothing in the passage describes a donor increasing its output in response to a drain.
These plants are presented as one unusual group, and paragraph 1 says most plants take up their own nutrients through a partnership.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Ectomycorrhizal and arbuscular partners differ mainly in their fungal lineages
The trade is well documented, the sharing between trees far less so
Isotope labelling has settled the question of how carbon moves between trees
Fungal networks join the trees of a forest into a single system of mutual care
Phosphate scarcity is the one force that has shaped the evolution of land plants

proof.quote: The trade of mineral nutrients for sugar and fat is measured and quantified.
What stays open is how much of that movement matters to a growing forest
the confident language of intention has run well ahead of the measurements
It is a partnership.

questions.why: The passage builds the partnership carefully, then spends its second half separating what the measurements show from what the popular story claims. Paragraph 17 states the split directly.
distractorNotes: The structural contrast is real, but it fills two paragraphs and is not what the passage is arguing.
Paragraph 11 and paragraph 17 both say the opposite: labelling raises a question the field has not closed.
This is the popular account the author pushes back on in paragraph 16, not the position the passage argues for.
Phosphate gets one paragraph as the reason the partnership pays, and the passage never claims it is the single driver of plant evolution.

questions.stem: Paragraph 12 is included mainly in order to
choices: argue that soil water supplies most of the nutrients in a forest
point out other ways a tag could reach a neighbouring plant
explain why root grafts form between trees of the same species
describe the way fallen leaves decompose on a forest floor
show that the fungal route carries more carbon than the soil route does

proof.quote: The network is also not the only road.
none requires a fungal conduit

questions.why: Paragraph 12 lists soil water, respired carbon dioxide, litter and root grafts, then says none of them requires a fungal conduit. Its job is to keep a tag in a neighbour from being read automatically as network traffic.
distractorNotes: Soil water is named as one possible path for a tag, not as the forest's main nutrient supply.
Grafts appear as one item on a list of alternative routes, and the passage never explains how or why they form.
Litter is mentioned in a single clause as a route, and paragraph 6 covers what litter contributes without describing decay.
Paragraph 12 makes no comparison of quantities. It says the routes are hard to tell apart, which is the opposite of ranking them.

questions.stem: The passage as a whole is organized as
choices: a problem raised in the opening and fully solved by the closing paragraph
a comparison of two fungal groups, followed by a defence of one of them
a series of experiments presented in the order they were carried out
a chronological history of research into the fungi of forest soils
an account of a partnership, then a limit on what it shows

proof.quote: It is a partnership.
The reason a tree pays for either arrangement
This is the point where care is required
What stays open is how much of that movement matters

questions.why: The first eight paragraphs build the symbiosis and price it. Paragraphs 9 and 10 give the method. From paragraph 11 on, the passage tests how far the results can be pushed, and paragraph 17 leaves the question open.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 17 says plainly that the central question stays open, so nothing is solved at the close.
The two groups are compared, but the author never takes a side between them.
The labelling work fills two paragraphs and is described by design rather than by date.
Only paragraph 2 is historical, and the rest of the passage is not arranged by date.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the popular image of the forest as a web of nurture is best described as
choices: alert to its appeal but unconvinced by it
indifferent to whether the image is accurate
fully persuaded by the case that has been made for it
openly contemptuous of everyone who repeats it
amused that researchers have allowed the phrase to spread so widely

proof.quote: the appeal is easy to see
the confident language of intention has run well ahead of the measurements

questions.why: Paragraph 16 grants that the appeal is easy to see and that some of the image is defensible as metaphor, then says the language of intention has run well ahead of the measurements. That is acknowledgement followed by doubt.
distractorNotes: Accuracy is the author's central concern, which is what paragraphs 11 through 14 are built to test.
Paragraph 16 states the opposite, that the confident language has outrun what has been measured.
The author is critical of the claims, not of the people, and paragraph 16 concedes the image has real appeal.
Paragraph 16 treats the overreach as a serious problem with the literature rather than as something funny.

questions.stem: In the final paragraph, the author treats the unanswered questions about carbon sharing as
choices: a sign that the whole field has been oversold
evidence that the symbiosis itself has been misdescribed
a reason to set the subject aside for the time being
a problem that no instrument will ever be able to settle
an opening for further work rather than a flaw

proof.quote: None of this diminishes the science.
The gap is where the interesting work sits

questions.why: Paragraph 17 lists what is not in doubt, names what stays open, and then says the gap is where the interesting work sits. The uncertainty is framed as the place to go next.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 17 opens by saying none of this diminishes the science, so the criticism is aimed at one claim, not the field.
Paragraph 17 calls the symbiosis ancient, nearly universal and structurally elegant, which is the part it treats as settled.
The closing sentence points toward more work on the question, not away from the subject.
No such limit is claimed. The passage describes methods that are getting stricter, not methods that are failing.

questions.stem: The passage supports each of the following statements EXCEPT
choices: Some of the fungi that form mycorrhizas produce mushrooms on a forest floor
Fungi steer carbon toward the seedlings most closely related to the donor
Phosphate moves through soil slowly enough to leave a root short of it
There are plants that live without making any sugar of their own
A share of what a tree makes in a given week ends up in fungal tissue

proof.quote: diffuses so slowly that a root strips the millimetre or two around itself within days
many are the familiar mushrooms of forest floors
the fungi live on sugar made that week
make no sugar at all
Flow may be set by the fungus, or simply by which end of the connection is hungrier.
several of the most repeated claims rest on a handful of studies

questions.why: Paragraph 14 raises a return to a relative only as one of the things a donor would need to get back for the behaviour to persist. The passage never reports that fungi actually route carbon by kinship, and paragraph 13 says flow may be set by the fungus or by simple demand.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 4 supports this by naming boletes, amanitas, chanterelles and truffles as ectomycorrhizal fungi.
Paragraph 5 supports this: phosphate diffuses so slowly that a root creates its own depletion zone within days.
Paragraph 15 supports this with ghost pipe and a number of orchids, which make no sugar at all.
Paragraph 8 supports this with the girdling result, which shows the fungi living on sugar made that week.

questions.stem: A reader who wants to know how investigators let hyphae, but not roots, pass between two plants should look in which paragraph?
choices: Paragraph 5
Paragraph 8
Paragraph 9
Paragraph 10
Paragraph 12

proof.quote: a mesh whose pores admit hyphae but exclude roots

questions.why: Paragraph 10 is the one that describes the mesh whose pores admit hyphae and exclude roots, along with the rotating cylinder used to shear the hyphae that cross.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 5 compares the widths of roots, root hairs and hyphae, but describes no apparatus.
Paragraph 8 covers the carbon budget and the girdling result, not the design of a transfer experiment.
Paragraph 9 explains how a plant is labelled with an isotope, which is the step before the barrier is set up.
Paragraph 12 lists routes other than the fungal one, which is a different concern from blocking roots.

questions.stem: A birch seedling, potted alone with an established fungal partner, is kept in a dark room for ten days so that it makes no new sugar. Based on the passage, the flow of carbon to its fungal partner would most likely
choices: continue unchanged, since the phosphate trade is unaffected
fall away within days, long before the ten days are up
reverse, with the fungus now supplying sugar to the seedling
rise, as the seedling leans harder on its partner for nutrients
taper off slowly over weeks as stored reserves are drawn down

proof.quote: show the flow falling away within days
the fungi live on sugar made that week, not on stored reserves

questions.why: Paragraph 8 gives the rule: when girdling cuts off the sugar supply, the flow to the fungi falls away within days, because the fungi live on sugar made that week, not on stored reserves. A seedling making no sugar at all is the same situation, so expect the flow to drop within days.
distractorNotes: Phosphate moving up is the fungus's side of the trade. Paragraph 8 is about the sugar moving down, and that supply depends on sugar made that week.
Nothing in the passage has a fungus feeding sugar to an ordinary green plant, and the seedling is potted alone, so there is no neighbouring tree for the fungus to draw on.
The flow in paragraph 8 is set by what the leaves make. A seedling making nothing has nothing extra to send, however much it needs its partner.
Paragraph 8 says the flow falls within days, not weeks, and that the fungi do not live on stored reserves.
